Note · Tetlock — Superforecasting

3 min read791 wordsUpdated 2026-10-19notes/canon/canon-tetlock-superforecasting.md

Canon · Cluster: Risk, Uncertainty & Fragility · Maps to Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making)

  • Source: Philip Tetlock & Dan Gardner, Superforecasting (2015)
  • Core claim: Most expert predictions are barely better than chance — but a measurable minority (superforecasters) are consistently better, and what they do is learnable.
  • Framework — what superforecasters do:
  • Think in probabilities, not certainties (and use fine-grained numbers — 65%, not "likely").
  • Update incrementally as evidence arrives (many small Bayesian revisions, not flip-flops).
  • Decompose big questions into smaller tractable sub-questions (Fermi-ize them).
  • Actively seek disconfirming evidence and the outside view / base rate first.
  • Keep score on themselves (calibration: do my 70%s happen ~70% of the time?).
  • The enemies: overconfidence and ideological commitment (the "hedgehog" with one big idea loses to the "fox" who knows many things).
  • Applies when: any recurring judgment under uncertainty where you can later check the result — forecasts, risk calls, planning estimates.
  • Breaks when: it works best on specific, time-bound, resolvable questions ("will X happen by Q3?") — it has less to say about Taleb's true Black Swans, the unscorable fat-tail events (canon taleb black swan); the two camps genuinely disagree on how much of the world is forecastable. Calibration also needs volume + feedback to develop, which most real decisions don't provide. And good process still yields bad outcomes sometimes — judge the process, not the single result (canon mauboussin success equation).

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — MindScience 360, "Why Predictions Fail," youtube.com/watch?v=koXUnYBBKCo) The habit that transfers is the scorecard, and the transcript is blunt about why most people never build the skill: "In most organizations, forecasts are made and forgotten, so there is no measurement, no revision, and no improvement" (MindScience 360). The practitioner move is to make the commitment explicit as a number — "using numbers makes commitments explicit" — then keep "a small log of your probabilities and dates, so you can later compare confidence with reality." That single discipline is Munger's "avoid overconfidence" made operational (canon munger poor charlies almanack).

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Forecasting is reframed as a measurable, learnable skill, not a gift — "This approach treats forecasting as a measurable skill, not a mysterious gift reserved for famous pundits" (MindScience 360, "Why Predictions Fail | Use Probabilities Instead of Certainty"). The mechanism is calibration: "Calibration means that your eighty percent calls should occur about eighty percent of the time, not just feeling confident," paired with resolution — "staying near fifty-fifty avoids being wrong but also avoids being useful." The summary corpus echoes the trait stack: "intellectual humility… they are also highly curious and open-minded… their ability to think probabilistically" (POCKETUNI), i.e. the fox, not the hedgehog.
  • Real application (mined): the transcript's worked example is exactly the Rep — a tournament question with a clear deadline where "one person posts sixty percent repeatedly and never learns much. Another person revises from forty to fifty-five to seventy as facts change, and the score reflects that learning" (MindScience 360). The method: "begin by counting similar past votes" (the outside view / base rate), then "adjust that baseline for new factors like shifting alliances or public opinion, and compute a rough probability" (the inside view). Brier scores are the keeping-score tool: forecasts converted "into distances from what happened, so lower scores mean closer contact with reality."
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the cluster's Taleb side draws the hard line — fragility is "something that does not like variability… a nonlinear accelerated reaction up to the point of breaking" (The Swedish Investor, "ANTIFRAGILE SUMMARY"). Tetlock's scoreable, time-bound questions don't reach those fat-tail events — you don't calibrate a once-a-century earthquake. A second, quieter pushback: the BusinessPsychologyHub transcript notes Tetlock's own work shows people run different rationalities ("intuitive Economist… Theologian… prosecutor"), so a clean probability is only one worldview — sacred-value and rule-enforcement framings resist being Fermi-ized into a number.
  • Sources in corpus: MindScience 360 — "Why Predictions Fail | Use Probabilities Instead of Certainty" (youtube.com/watch?v=koXUnYBBKCo) · POCKETUNI — "Superforecasting… by Philip Tetlock" (youtube.com/watch?v=jOsc5cyeZO8) · BusinessPsychologyHub — "Decision making theorist Philip Tetlock (and rap star Jay Z)" (youtube.com/watch?v=GTwQaB68r0s) · The Swedish Investor — "ANTIFRAGILE SUMMARY (BY NASSIM TALEB)" (youtube.com/watch?v=-MMLea-_ifw). Rep

Make one real prediction this week as a number ("60% we hit the deadline"). Write it down. When it resolves, check it. Repeat — that loop is the skill.
